---
title: "Z-Score Normalization"
description: "A feature transformation that expresses values in standard-deviation units relative to a mean."
term: "Z-Score Normalization"
letter: "Z"
category: "Statistics"
difficulty: "Beginner"
---

## Simple explanation

Z-score normalization subtracts a feature's mean and divides by its standard
deviation, expressing each value in units of typical variation.

## Technical explanation

For a value $x$, mean $\mu$, and standard deviation $\sigma>0$, its z-score is
$z=(x-\mu)/\sigma$. In machine learning, estimate $\mu$ and $\sigma$ using the
training data only, then reuse those values to transform validation, test, and
production data. This prevents information leakage and ensures consistent
scaling.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Scaling can improve optimization for models sensitive to feature magnitude
and makes different numerical ranges easier to compare. It does not make
features normally distributed, remove outliers, or guarantee improved
performance for every model.

## How it works

Compute per-feature means and standard deviations on the training partition.
Transform values using those statistics. Handle constant or near-constant
features explicitly, and consider robust scaling when outliers dominate the
mean and standard deviation.

## Practical example

Fit a standard scaler on the training rows of a dataset, then use the fitted
scaler to transform validation and test rows. Do not independently recompute
the mean and standard deviation on each split.

## Common misconceptions

- Z-score scaling does not clip outliers; extreme values remain extreme in
  standardized units.
- A z-score is not automatically a probability or a percentile unless
  distributional assumptions are justified.
